extracted.intended_audience: general readers, educators, content creators, and clinicians interested in trauma triggers and trigger warnings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and explanatory criteria about what trauma triggers are, common types of triggers, and how/when to use trigger or content warnings (especially in educational and media contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a trauma trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: A trauma trigger is a psychological stimulus that prompts involuntary recall of a previous traumatic experience; the stimulus itself need not be frightening or traumatic and may be only indirectly or superficially reminiscent of an earlier incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triggers can be subtle, individual, and difficult for others to predict; the process of connecting experience to a trigger is called 'traumatic coupling'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of triggered responses
rubrics_metrics.description: When trauma is 'triggered', the involuntary response can go far beyond discomfort and include overwhelming, uncontrollable reactions such as panic attacks, flashbacks, or strong impulses to flee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that triggered responses may need clinical attention and are not merely emotional sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance as a symptom and treatment implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoiding trauma triggers is a common behavioral symptom of PTSD and related disorders; long-term avoidance increases the likelihood of developing disabling PTSD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying and addressing trauma triggers is an important part of treating PTSD; avoid encouraging long-term avoidance as a coping strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common types of triggers (sensory and contextual examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Triggers can include particular smells, tastes, sounds (e.g., helicopters, songs), textures, times of day or year, sights (real, photo, film, video), places, people, arguments, skin sensations, body position, physical pain, emotions, and particular situations (e.g., crowded places).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trigger is usually personal and specific and need not be closely related to the actual experience (e.g., a motorbike sound associated with sirens). Provide concrete examples to help recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Olfaction and traumatic reminders
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of smell (olfaction) may be more closely connected to traumatic reminders than other sensory experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider smells as especially salient triggers when assessing or preventing re-exposure for survivors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and distinction: trigger warning vs content warning
rubrics_metrics.description: A trigger warning is a message presented to an audience that a piece of media contains potentially distressing content; 'content warning' is a more generic term not directly focused on PTSD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'content warning' for broader advisory notices (e.g., TV parental guidelines) and 'trigger warning' when specifically aimed at trauma-related reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical format for warnings in non-fiction media
rubrics_metrics.description: In non-fiction books and online videos, trigger warnings can be specific to chapters or segments and provide timestamps and page numbers to allow audiences to skip only certain parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing precise locations (timestamps/page numbers) is recommended to enable selective avoidance without forfeiting the entire work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of warnings in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: In works of fiction, skipping certain parts can disrupt narrative flow, making it more difficult to provide effective segment-specific warnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that strategies effective in non-fiction (segment-specific warnings) may not translate well to fiction without harming the audience's experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable accommodations in educational contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is broad agreement on providing reasonable accommodations for a small number of students (e.g., current/former military personnel, sexual assault survivors) whose disabling PTSD impairs learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include mentioning in advance detailed descriptions of violence or warning about demonstrations that will produce loud sounds; accommodations should be targeted and individualized rather than blanket course censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and pedagogical considerations in higher education
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of general content or trigger warnings in university curricula is contested: critics say they infantilize students and prioritize comfort over intellectual engagement; supporters view warnings as pedagogical tools to prepare students or provide alternate learning modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should weigh academic freedom and resilience-building against legitimate needs for accommodations; policies vary by university (e.g., University of Chicago opposed, UC Santa Barbara supportive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence on effectiveness of trigger warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Research suggests trigger warnings are neither harmful nor especially helpful overall: among people without traumatic experiences warnings did not affect anxiety; for those with PTSD warnings had little statistically significant effect and effect sizes on negative outcomes have been 'trivial'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies indicate most students read triggering passages even when alternatives are offered, and short- and medium-term harms from exposure are not consistently increased; rely on empirical findings rather than assumptions when designing warning policies.
